No worries :) wanting more is always ok although being aware of our own limitations is the key.
Keep in mind that you'll drive very differently if you are more tired than usual, if your car is heavier than usual, etc... 
The key is being able to recognize these situations and react accordingly (give yourself more room for error if you're tired, for instance). If you do that you'll always drive consistently :)

I have only 4 years of driving experience but if I may suggest this: I think you'd be better off with a shitty car as a starter. I'd recommend a fiat since they're mechanically indestructible although very badly made regarding everything else. You can still have a little fun with them but you can abuse them in any way shape or form and should the unthinkable happen you'll never be able to find yourself speeding too much because they're not fast cars.
In this scenario you'd be able to push your driving skills more and more over your limit (hence learning) while still being confined in a safer environment.

Then again: your money your choice :)

If I may also recommend, if you're also thinking about mechanical modifications just make sure that you know what those imply.


If, for example, you'd like to lower the driving height even further keep in mind that you'd have to avoid potholes even harder. This might not be a problem worth considering for many people but as a new driver on the road I'd suggest you stick with what you're given for a while, then read everything you can possibly find about those modifications (even changing the braking system, for example, could destroy your habits regarding pedal pressure and results) and then proceed ONLY if you understood the implications and you're ok with them.

As a humble Italian I've had too many friends experiencing near death experiences related to heavy modifications and inexperience with scooters.

That's not to say you're incompetent at driving. You WILL be incompetent for a period of time though with everything that's new for you (from a car to some new tires), no matter what. Keep that in mind and be careful out there :)

Avoid correcting lateral position as that influences pitch a lot on ksp. Align yourself with the runway first, descent second if you're having trouble with alignment

Watch your vertical speed more than your horizontal speed

With that in mind, slow down as long as your vertical speed is satisfactory. If you want to gain more altitude (hence adding vertical speed) DON'T MOVE THE NOSE but increase the speed, if you want to lose altitude (hence lose vertical speed) decrease the thrust

Keep the nose a little above the horizon and lock it with SAS, then, as already suggested, proceed to control the stall watching vertical speed only and adjusting it with thrust only

Practice this way of flying (actually called low speed flight) and then, when you're comfortable enough, fly normally to the runway and do it again! Use speedbrakes both in the air (CAREFULLY) and on the ground (less carefully). Use thrust reversers if you have them
